title: Cap. III Rat. 13: absolute election evacuates hortation, correction, prayer, industry — Pelagian charge
latin: Rat. 13. Aliud argumentum huic affine est, quod etiam ab antiquis Pelagianis vibrari solebat in Augustinum; nimirum, Hanc doctrinam de electione absoluta singularum personarum ante praevisionem meritorum, hortationem omnem et correptionem evacuare, orationes inutiles facere, omnem industriam exstinguere, desperationem denique hominibus inferre. Haec apud Augustinum videre licet, De bono perseverantiae lib. 2. cap. 16. et 17. et 23. et per totum fere librum De correptione et gratia. Ex epistolis etiam Hilarii et Prosperi, quae extant inter Augustini Opera, Tom. 7. patet fuisse haec omnia invidiose objecta Augustino a Pelagianis. Quinetiam apud ipsum Faustum Regiensem haec omnia occurrunt, lib. 1. sect. 9. et 10. et passim per illud plenum veneni et pestilentiae scriptum. Summa omnium est; Ex hac sententia nostra, salutem ingerendam esse electis sive nihil agentibus, sive male agentibus, denegandam esse non-electis quantumvis laborantibus et pie viventibus.
pass_a: Reason 13. Another argument akin to this is what the ancient Pelagians also used to brandish against Augustine; namely, That this doctrine of the absolute election of singular persons before the foresight of merits empties every hortation and correction, makes prayers useless, extinguishes all industry, and finally brings despair upon men. These things may be seen in Augustine, On the Good of Perseverance book 2 chapters 16 and 17 and 23, and through nearly the whole book On Correction and Grace. From the letters also of Hilary and Prosper, which stand among Augustine's Works, Tom. 7, it is plain that all these things were invidiously objected to Augustine by the Pelagians. Moreover in Faustus of Riez himself all these things occur, book 1 sections 9 and 10, and throughout that writing full of poison and pestilence. The sum of all is: From this our sentence, salvation is to be thrust upon the elect whether they do nothing or do ill, and is to be denied to the non-elect however much they labor and live piously.
pass_b: Rat. 13. Another argument akin to this the ancient Pelagians also used to brandish against Augustine: namely, that this doctrine of absolute election of singular persons before foresight of merits empties every hortation and correction, makes prayers useless, extinguishes all industry, and finally brings despair on men. See Augustine, De bono perseverantiae 2.16, 17, 23, and nearly the whole of De correptione et gratia. From Hilary's and Prosper's letters among Augustine's Works (Tom. 7) it is plain the Pelagians objected all this invidiously. The same runs through Faustus of Riez, book 1 sect. 9 and 10, and that writing full of poison and pestilence. Sum of it: on our sentence, salvation is thrust on the elect whether idle or wicked, and denied to the non-elect however hard they labor and live piously.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13: Augustine dissolves — election excites industry; despair is the impious' vice
latin: Sol. Haec omnia dissolvuntur ab Augustino in locis modo citatis; Respondeo tamen, doctrinam electionis in piis omnibus excitare, et incendere industriam bene vivendi. Quod si impii et profani inde occasionem torporis aut desperationis accipiant, id fieri illorum vitio et innata perversitate, non ipsius doctrinae.
pass_a: Solution. All these things are dissolved by Augustine in the places just cited; I answer nonetheless that the doctrine of election in all the pious excites and kindles the industry of living well. But if the impious and profane take thence occasion of torpor or despair, that happens by their vice and innate perversity, not by the doctrine itself.
pass_b: Sol. Augustine dissolves all this in the places just cited. Still I answer: the doctrine of election excites and kindles industry of living well in all the pious. If the impious and profane take from it occasion of torpor or despair, that is their vice and innate perversity — not the doctrine's.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13: same occasion from divine foresight — Augustine De bono pers. 2.15
latin: Atque similem prorsus occasionem desumi posse ex doctrina praescientiae Divinae (quam tamen nemo nisi atheus, aut valde imperitus rejicit) demonstravit Augustinus, De bono perseverantiae lib. 2. cap. 15.
pass_a: And that a wholly similar occasion can be taken from the doctrine of the Divine foresight (which nonetheless no one except an atheist, or one greatly unskilled, rejects) Augustine has demonstrated, On the Good of Perseverance book 2 chapter 15.
pass_b: And Augustine showed (De bono perseverantiae 2.15) that a wholly similar occasion can be taken from the doctrine of divine foresight — which no one but an atheist, or one greatly unskilled, rejects.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13: nearer point — gratuitous election stabilizes hortations as ordained media
latin: Sed propius ad rem, Dico, hac doctrina gratuitae electionis stabiliri hortationes et correptiones, incendi hominum voluntates ad pie vivendum; quia sic arcanam Dei de eligendis certis hominibus voluntatem praedicamus, ut simul revelatam ejus voluntatem non taceamus, quae hosce electos non nisi per media a Deo ordinata ad finem illis destinatum perducendos decrevit. Hortationes autem, correptiones, orationes, et id genus alia, ab omnibus habentur inter illa media, quae promovendae electorum saluti Divina sapientia ordinavit.
pass_a: But nearer to the matter, I say that by this doctrine of gratuitous election hortations and corrections are stabilized, and men's wills are kindled to living piously; because we so preach the secret will of God concerning electing certain men, that at the same time we do not keep silent about his revealed will, which has decreed that these elect are to be led to the end destined for them only through means ordained by God. But hortations, corrections, prayers, and things of that kind are held by all among those means which the Divine wisdom has ordained for promoting the elect's salvation.
pass_b: Nearer the point: I say this doctrine of gratuitous election stabilizes hortations and corrections and kindles men's wills to live piously — because we preach God's secret will to elect certain persons without silencing his revealed will, which decrees those elect are led to their destined end only through means God ordained. Hortations, corrections, prayers, and the like are among those means Divine wisdom ordained to promote the elect's salvation.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 13 close: no despair for the willing — removes boasting, not study of holiness
latin: Neque ulli mortalium volenti credere et pie vivere desperationem injicimus, sed certissimam fiduciam talibus praebemus, eos pertinere ad numerum electorum et salvandorum. Nam sic praedicamus gratuitam electionem, ut simul doceamus neminem posse vel fructum vel solatium inde percipere absque fide et sanctitate: quemlibet autem fideliter et sancte viventem posse ac debere seipsum in electis numerare. Haec igitur doctrina electionis tollit homini omnem gloriandi et superbiendi de suis operibus occasionem, sed non tollit ipsum studium bene operandi; quin excitat potius, dum docet, neminem aut certitudinem ullam habere de sua electione extra studium sanctitatis, aut unquam ad finem electionis, id est, vitam aeternam, pervenire posse nisi per viam sanctitatis.
pass_a: Nor do we inject despair into any mortal willing to believe and live piously, but we offer such persons most certain confidence that they belong to the number of the elect and of those to be saved. For we so preach gratuitous election that at the same time we teach that no one can perceive fruit or consolation from it without faith and holiness: but that anyone living faithfully and holily can and ought to number himself among the elect. This doctrine of election therefore takes away from a man every occasion of boasting and pride about his works, but does not take away the study itself of doing well; rather it excites it, while it teaches that no one has any certainty of his election outside the study of holiness, or can ever arrive at the end of election, that is eternal life, except through the way of holiness.
pass_b: Nor do we cast despair on any mortal willing to believe and live piously: we give such people most sure confidence they belong among the elect and those to be saved. We preach gratuitous election while teaching that no one gets fruit or comfort from it without faith and holiness — and that anyone living faithfully and holily can and ought to count himself among the elect. So the doctrine takes away every occasion of boasting and pride in one's works, but not the study of doing well; it rather kindles that study, teaching that no one has any certainty of election outside pursuit of holiness, or can ever reach election's end — eternal life — except by the way of holiness.
